A corpse is the dead body of a human being. The very moment a person dies, their physical body becomes a corpse. That's the single most important thing to know: the word refers to a human body that is no longer alive.

A corpse is the whole, physical body — flesh, bones, and all — as it exists after death. It is not a ghost, not a soul, not a memory of the person. It is the tangible, material body that is left behind when life ends. Typically, the word is used to describe a body that is still mostly intact, not yet fully decomposed into only bones.

Mostly, yes. "Corpse" is used almost exclusively for human beings. When an animal dies, its dead body is generally called a carcass, not a corpse. However, in literature or informal speech, you will occasionally see "corpse" extended to animals, especially to create a more serious or dramatic tone.
How the word feels — its tone

"Corpse" is a serious, weighty word. It is not rude or offensive, but it is direct and carries a somber gravity. It sounds clinical and factual, which is why you often encounter it in crime reporting, police investigations, medical contexts, and literature. Saying "a corpse was found" sounds more formal and stark than saying "a body was found," though both are correct.
How it compares to similar words

It helps a lot to know how "corpse" sits among similar words:

Body is the most general and neutral word. You can say "the body of the deceased" and it feels respectful and soft. "Corpse" is slightly more blunt and clinical.

Cadaver is a near-synonym, but it has a very specific home: the medical and scientific world. When doctors or students study a dead human body for anatomy, surgery training, or research, they call it a cadaver. Outside of that scientific setting, "cadaver" sounds out of place. "Corpse" is the everyday, general word; "cadaver" is the specialized medical one.

Remains is a softer, more respectful word often used when speaking of a person who has passed away, especially when time has passed and the body is no longer intact — just bones, ashes, or fragments. "Remains" is what you might hear at a funeral or in a eulogy. A "corpse" is more immediate and concrete.

Carcass, as mentioned, is for animals. Using it for a human would sound callous or insulting.
The key moment the word applies

"Corpse" applies the instant a living person dies. A living person, no matter how sick, is never a corpse. A person who appears dead but is still alive is not a corpse. The word only applies after death is confirmed. This is why in crime fiction and detective stories, investigators talk about finding a corpse — it marks the moment death has occurred and the investigation begins.

"Corpse" is occasionally used figuratively — meaning it can describe something that is no longer alive in a broader, non-literal sense. For example: "That business is a corpse — nothing can save it now." Here, the speaker means the business is completely dead and finished, beyond any recovery. This usage borrows the stark finality of the word to describe something that has totally collapsed or ceased to function.

To see the word in action:

  • "The police discovered a corpse near the river early in the morning."
  • "Historians estimated that thousands of corpses were buried in the unmarked field."
  • "The scene in the play required one actor to lie completely still and play the role of a corpse."
  • "She examined the corpse carefully before writing her medical report."

"Corpse" focuses entirely on the physical. It says nothing about who the person was, how they lived, or how they died. It is a neutral, descriptive label for what remains of a human being after life has left it. That neutrality — that purely physical focus — is exactly what makes the word useful in formal, legal, and scientific contexts where objectivity matters.
